small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Properties of number_9_Lowest common multiple (LCM)
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of multiples to find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers. Encourage a systematic approach when listing multiples, and discuss with students that, while multiples are infinite, they only need to list enough to identify a common one. Prompt them to highlight any common multiples before identifying the lowest common multiple. Once confident, students can progress to word problems and examples involving more than two numbers. Discuss the difference between the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple, helping students to understand when each one is used. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple. • Students may assume that the product of the two numbers is the lowest common multiple, for example that 36 is the lowest common multiple of 3 and 12 • Students may incorrectly list the multiples of two numbers. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 2 – Properties of numbers | Step 9 Mathematical talk • List the first ten multiples of • What are some common multiples of and ? • What is the lowest common multiple of and ? • Explain why the product of two numbers will be a common multiple of the numbers. • When is the lowest common multiple of two numbers not the same as their product? • Do all pairs of numbers have a lowest common multiple? Explain how you know. • Can the lowest common multiple of two numbers ever be the same as one of the numbers? Explain how you know. • Is it possible to work out the highest common multiple? Explain how you know. National Curriculum links • Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (or divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers by listing multiples systematically. They identify common multiples and distinguish between the highest common factor and LCM. Address misconceptions, such as confusing LCM with the product of numbers. Progress to solving word problems involving more than two numbers.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Properties of number_10_HCF and LCM from a Venn diagram (E)
small_step_name: HCF and LCM from a Venn diagram (E)
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students build on previous learning to use Venn diagrams to find the highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM). Ensure that students are confident in expressing numbers as a product of their prime factors before introducing this method. Model how to represent the prime factors of two numbers in a Venn diagram, emphasising that the intersection shows the shared prime factors. Explain that multiplying the numbers in the intersection gives the highest common factor, while multiplying all the numbers in the Venn diagram gives the lowest common multiple. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse which factors are multiplied to calculate the highest common factor or the lowest common multiple. • Students may duplicate prime factors in the Venn diagrams when they appear in both numbers. • Students may not understand that if there are no common prime factors in the intersection, then the highest common factor is 1 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 2 – Properties of numbers | Step 10 Mathematical talk • Express as a product of its prime factors. • Where in the Venn diagram do you write the common prime factors? • How do you calculate the highest common factor from a Venn diagram? • How do you calculate the lowest common multiple from a Venn diagram? • Explain why multiplying all the prime factors in the Venn diagram gives the lowest common multiple. • If two numbers have no common prime factors, what does the intersection of the Venn diagram contain? What does this tell you about their highest common factor? • What is the highest common factor when there are no common prime factors in the intersection of the Venn diagram? E National Curriculum links • Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (or divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property
candidate_ss_desc: Students use Venn diagrams to find the highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM) by representing numbers as products of their prime factors. The intersection shows shared prime factors for HCF, while multiplying all factors gives the LCM. Address misconceptions about factor placement and calculation errors.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Properties of number_11_Use factors to simplify calculations (E)
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students develop flexibility in representing numbers by expressing them as a product of factors to simplify calculations. Encourage students to rewrite numbers in ways that make mental or written methods more efficient. For example, in the calculation 16 × 50, students could express 16 as 4 × 4 and 50 as 25 × 2, recognising that 4 × 25 = 100 and so simplifying the calculation to 100 × 4 × 2. Discuss the commutative property of multiplication, showing how reordering factors can make calculations easier. The focus is not on prime factorisation but on selecting factor groupings that simplify the process, helping students to develop efficient strategies for working without a calculator. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write a value as a product of its prime factors, without considering how other representations may be more efficient. • Students may attempt to calculate the products in the order they are given, rather than looking for useful factor pairs that simplify the calculation, such as numbers that multiply to make 10 or 100 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 2 – Properties of numbers | Step 11 Mathematical talk • What are some useful factors of a number to identify? • Why is it useful to identify pairs of factors that multiply to give 10 or 100? • Write as a product of its factors. • Is writing a value as a product of its prime factors always the most efficient method? Explain how you know. • How many different ways can you express as a product of its factors? • Which product of factors is the most efficient for the calculation? Explain how you know. • Explain why multiplying the factors in any order still gives the same answer. E National Curriculum links • Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (or divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to express numbers as a product of factors to simplify calculations, enhancing mental or written methods. For example, in 16 × 50, express 16 as 4 × 4 and 50 as 25 × 2, simplifying to 100 × 4 × 2. Focus on efficient factor groupings, not prime factorisation, and discuss the commutative property of multiplication.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Add and subtract fractions_9_Add and subtract simple algebraic fractions (E)
small_step_name: Add and subtract simple algebraic fractions (E)
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students further develop their understanding of fractions within the context of algebra. Start by comparing the addition of fractional expressions to the addition of fractions in numerical form, keeping examples simple at this introductory stage, rather than using complex multi-term expressions. Provide practice with algebraic fractions that include variables in both numerators and denominators. If necessary, revisit the process of adding and subtracting fractions with different denominators before extending to algebraic cases. Where appropriate, challenge students with equations equal to a whole involving algebraic fractions, for example 3 x + 2 x = 1 Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not make the denominators equal before adding or subtracting the fractions. • Students may struggle to identify common denominators when the denominators are algebraic. • Students may incorrectly convert an expression into a fraction before adding or subtracting, for example x + 3x 4 = x x + 3x 4 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 3 – Add and subtract fractions | Step 9 National Curriculum links • Use the four operations, including formal written methods, applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative • Use and interpret algebraic notation, including: ab in place of a × b; 3y in place of y + y + y and 3 × y; a2 in place of a × a, a3 in place of a × a × a; a2b in place of a × a × b; a b in place of a ÷ b; coefficients written as fractions rather than as decimals; brackets Mathematical talk • What is meant by “like terms”? • What is the same and what is different about 1 2 + 1 2 and a 2 + a 2 ? • How can you rewrite 3 x + 1 2x with equivalent denominators? • What is the same and what is different about x 4 and 1 4 x? • What does “in terms of m” mean? • Can the fraction be simplified? Explain your answer. • What must the value of y be if 2 y + 5 y = 1? Explain how you know. E
candidate_ss_desc: Students extend their understanding of fractions in algebra by comparing the addition of fractional expressions to numerical fractions. Practice involves algebraic fractions with variables in numerators and denominators. Address misconceptions such as not equalizing denominators before adding. Challenge students with equations involving algebraic fractions equaling a whole, e.g., 3x + 2x = 1.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Add and subtract fractions_10_Substitution and solving equations with fractions (E)
small_step_name: Substitution and solving equations with fractions (E)
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students apply their knowledge of adding and subtracting algebraic fractions within algebraic contexts, including substitution and solving equations. Start by focusing on substituting values into a range of algebraic fractional expressions. It may be helpful to revisit substitution in expressions without fractions before extending to those that include them. Similarly, when solving equations, recap methods for one- and two-step equations before introducing fractional terms, to support understanding. Where appropriate, provide additional challenge by including fractions greater than 1 in substitution problems or equations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may apply the incorrect inverse operation when solving equations. • Students may make errors when substituting into expressions with powers, for example treating p2 as “double p” instead of squaring the value of p. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 3 – Add and subtract fractions | Step 10 National Curriculum links • Use the four operations, including formal written methods, applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative • Substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions, including scientific formulae • Use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable (including all forms that require rearrangement) Mathematical talk • What is the value of the expression if x = ? • Is it possible to substitute fractions into algebraic expressions? Explain your answer. • What is the inverse of ? • What is a possible first step to solving the equation? • What calculation is equivalent to x2? • Can you collect any like terms before beginning to solve the equation? Explain your answer. • Can the value of an unknown be both negative and fractional? Explain your answer. E
candidate_ss_desc: Students apply their knowledge of adding and subtracting algebraic fractions, focusing on substitution and solving equations. Begin with substituting values into algebraic fractional expressions, then solve equations with fractional terms. Address misconceptions, such as incorrect inverse operations and errors in substituting powers. Challenge students with fractions greater than 1 in problems.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Angles and polygons_9_Solve problems with angles
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply known angle facts to calculate unknown angles in a variety of contexts. At this stage, students should be confident in using all the angle facts covered so far in this block. The focus of this step is on identifying which fact to apply and justifying solutions using accurate mathematical vocabulary and notation. Encourage students to explain their thinking clearly and to check whether their answers are sensible. Model how to set up and solve equations based on different angle facts. More challenging questions may combine several angle facts, requiring a step-by- step approach to reach the solution. Calculators can be used to ensure that the focus remains on the application of the angle facts, rather than the arithmetic. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse which fact or facts apply to a situation. • Students may forget that vertically opposite angles are equal and instead assume that they sum to 180° or 360°. • Students may try to measure rather than calculate angles. • Students may not show clear reasoning or may use incorrect or incomplete justification when explaining their answers. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 9 Mathematical talk • What do you know? What can you find out? • What information can you add to the diagram? • How do you decide which angle fact to use and apply? • Is it possible to apply more than one angle fact in this problem? • Which angle facts do you know? • Which angle facts do you think you will need to apply to this problem? • How do you know whether to use 180° or 360° in a calculation? • How can you check that your answer is sensible once you have calculated an unknown angle? National Curriculum links • Apply the properties of angles at a point, angles at a point on a straight line, vertically opposite angles • Derive and use the sum of angles in a triangle and use it to deduce the angle sum in any polygon, and to derive properties of regular polygons • Apply angle facts, triangle congruence, similarity and properties of quadrilaterals to derive results about angles and sides, including Pythagoras’ theorem, and use known results to obtain simple proofs
candidate_ss_desc: Students apply known angle facts to calculate unknown angles in various contexts, focusing on identifying and justifying the correct fact to use. They should clearly explain their reasoning and check their answers. This step involves setting up equations and may combine multiple angle facts. Calculators are used to emphasize understanding angle facts over arithmetic.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Angles and polygons_10_Parallel and perpendicular lines
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate and extend their Key Stage 2 understanding of parallel and perpendicular lines. Remind students that parallel lines are always the same distance apart and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle (90°), which can be shown using a square corner or set square. Use clear diagrams and practical examples, such as train tracks for parallel lines or the corner of a book for perpendicular lines. Encourage students to spot these relationships in shapes, coordinate grids and the classroom environment. Emphasise accurate vocabulary, such as “intersect” and “right angle”, and correct notation, including arrows for parallel lines and squares for right angles. Students should practise drawing parallel and perpendicular lines using a ruler and protractor or set square. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that all lines that do not meet are parallel, overlooking the fact that parallel lines must also be equidistant. • Students may assume that lines need to be the same length to be parallel. • Students may confuse perpendicular lines with any intersecting lines. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 10 Mathematical talk • How can you tell that two lines are parallel? • What does it mean for two lines to be the same distance apart? • Can parallel lines ever meet? Explain your answer. • What makes a pair of lines perpendicular? • How can you check that two lines are perpendicular? • What is the same and what is different about parallel lines and perpendicular lines? • Where might you see parallel/perpendicular lines in everyday life? • If line AB is perpendicular to CD, and EF is parallel to AB, what is the relationship between EF and CD? National Curriculum links • Describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations: points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, right angles, regular polygons, and other polygons that are reflectively and rotationally symmetric
candidate_ss_desc: Students consolidate their understanding of parallel and perpendicular lines. Parallel lines are equidistant and never meet, while perpendicular lines intersect at a right angle (90°). Use diagrams and examples, like train tracks and book corners, to illustrate. Emphasize accurate vocabulary and notation. Practice drawing with a ruler and protractor. Address misconceptions about line properties.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Angles and polygons_11_Investigate angles in parallel lines  E
small_step_name: Investigate angles in parallel lines  E
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore angles formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines. The focus of this step is on careful measurement and observation of angles in parallel lines. Students investigate patterns and compare different angle positions. Encourage them to use known angle facts, such as angles on a straight line or around a point, to justify their ideas, where possible. Provide opportunities for students to test their conjectures with further examples to build confidence. This investigative approach develops curiosity and provides a secure foundation for introducing formal parallel line angle facts in later steps. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that all angles formed by a transversal and parallel lines are equal. • Students may believe that parallel lines must always be horizontal. • Students may not understand that there can be more than two parallel lines in a set. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 11 Mathematical talk • How can you identify parallel lines? • Do parallel lines always have to be drawn horizontally? Explain your answer. • How many angles are created when a transversal intersects a pair of parallel lines? • What do you notice about the sizes of the angles formed between a transversal and parallel lines? Is there a pattern? • Are there any other pairs of equal angles? Explain how you know. • If you know the size of one angle, how can you use angles on a straight line, vertically opposite angles and angles around a point to work out other angles? National Curriculum links • Apply the properties of angles at a point, angles at a point on a straight line, vertically opposite angles • Understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles • Describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations: points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, right angles, regular polygons, and other polygons that are reflectively and rotationally symmetric E
candidate_ss_desc: Students explore angles formed when a transversal intersects parallel lines, focusing on measurement and observation. They investigate patterns, using known angle facts like angles on a straight line, to justify ideas. This step builds a foundation for formal parallel line angle facts. Misconceptions include assuming all angles are equal or parallel lines must be horizontal.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Angles and polygons_12_Angles in any polygon  E
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students are introduced to the sum of the interior angles in a polygon. Start with triangles, where the angles sum to 180°, and quadrilaterals, which can be split into two triangles to give 360°. Explore polygons with more sides by partitioning them into triangles from a single vertex, for example splitting a pentagon into three triangles, making the sum of the interior angles 540°. Encourage students to investigate different polygons and record their findings, noticing how the number of sides links to the number of triangles and the total angle sum. Then introduce regular polygons, showing how each interior angle can be found by dividing the total by the number of sides. Students also identify interior and exterior angles at a vertex and calculate them using their knowledge of angles on a straight line. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that the sum of the interior angles differs between regular and irregular polygons. • Students may assume that the sum of the angles can be found by multiplying the number of sides by 180°. • Students may struggle to split the polygons into triangles, using more than one vertex. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 12 Mathematical talk • How many triangles can a quadrilateral be split into? What does that tell you about the total sum of its interior angles? • If a pentagon can be split into three triangles, what does that tell you about the total sum of its interior angles? • Why is the interior angle sum of any polygon always a multiple of 180°? • Describe the relationship between the number of sides a polygon has and the number of triangles it can be split into from one vertex. • How can you calculate the angle sum of any polygon? Does your method work for concave polygons? National Curriculum links • Derive and use the sum of angles in a triangle and use it to deduce the angle sum in any polygon, and to derive properties of regular polygons E
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn the sum of interior angles in polygons, starting with triangles (180°) and quadrilaterals (360°). They partition polygons into triangles from a single vertex to find the angle sum, e.g., a pentagon into three triangles (540°). Explore regular polygons by dividing the total angle sum by the number of sides. Calculate interior and exterior angles using angles on a straight line.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Angles and polygons_13_Simple proofs  E
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students are introduced to the idea of simple proofs using known angle facts. Distinguish between a demonstration, which shows why something is true in one case, and a proof, which explains why it is always true. Model how the angles in a triangle sum to 180° by cutting out the three corners and rearranging them so that they fit together along a straight line. Encourage students to make links to earlier angle facts, recognising that angles on a straight line sum to 180°. Students should practise writing short proofs, focusing on clear reasoning and step-by-step justification. Discussions about efficiency and generalisation will help students to see how proofs provide certainty and are more powerful than examples alone. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that showing one example is enough to prove a fact. • Students may think that proofs are only shown by calculations, rather than reasoning and logical facts. • Students may write explanations without a clear structure. • Students may struggle with more challenging expressions such as 180 − (90 − x). Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 13 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about a proof and a demonstration? • What do you know? What can you find out? • Is it possible to prove something in more than one way? • How could you prove that there are 360° in a full turn? • Why is it important to write each step of a proof in order? • This trapezium has two right angles. Does this mean that every trapezium has two right angles? Explain how you know. • How can you prove that the angles in a pentagon sum to 540° using the fact that angles in a triangle sum to 180°? National Curriculum links • Apply angle facts, triangle congruence, similarity and properties of quadrilaterals to derive results about angles and sides, including Pythagoras’ theorem, and use known results to obtain simple proofs E
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn simple proofs using known angle facts, distinguishing between demonstrations and proofs. They model how triangle angles sum to 180° and practice writing proofs with clear reasoning. Discussions on efficiency and generalization highlight proof certainty. Address misconceptions about examples and proof structure. National Curriculum links include applying angle facts and deriving results.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_1_Basic angle rules and notation
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students review the basic rules of angles and notation covered in Year 7 Start by looking at each rule in isolation: the sum of angles on a straight line, angles around a point and angles in triangles and quadrilaterals. Students should be able to identify when angles sum to 180° or 360° and when angles are equal. Once they are confident in identifying the correct rule, move on to diagrams where more than one rule may need to be applied. Remind students of the three-letter angle notation, which is used throughout the block. Encourage them to explain and justify how they identify and calculate angles, using correct vocabulary and angle rules. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the different rules relating to angles in lines and shapes. • Students may confuse instances when angles sum to 180° and when they sum to 360°. • Students may believe that angles on the same straight line that do not meet still sum to 180°. • In their calculations, students may not account for angles that are not labelled. Year 8 | Summer term | Block 1 – Angles in parallel lines and polygons | Step 1 National Curriculum links • Use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC, and know and use the criteria for congruence of triangles • Apply the properties of angles at a point, angles at a point on a straight line, vertically opposite angles Mathematical talk • What is the sum of the angles on a straight line? • In which shape do the interior angles sum to 360°? • A triangle has angles of ° and °. What is the size of the third angle? • What is the difference between an acute angle and an obtuse angle? • In the angle notation ABC, the intersection of the lines forming the angle will be labelled with which letter? • Vertically opposite angles are • Angles in a triangle sum to °. • Angles in a quadrilateral sum to °.
candidate_ss_desc: Students review angle rules: angles on a straight line sum to 180°, angles around a point sum to 360°, and angles in triangles and quadrilaterals. They apply these rules to diagrams, using three-letter angle notation and correct vocabulary. Misconceptions include confusing angle sums and neglecting unlabelled angles.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Tables and probability_9_Probabilities from two-way tables
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use two-way tables to calculate probabilities. Model how to extract relevant information from a two-way table to work out probabilities. Emphasise the importance of carefully reading the question and identifying the correct values, highlighting which total to divide by, as this may be the total for the entire table or a specific row or column total, depending on the wording and focus of the question. Reinforce accurate probability notation and remind students to express their answers as fractions, decimals or percentages. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misread the table and select the wrong cell for an outcome. • Students may use the number of times an outcome does not happen as the denominator of a fraction when calculating probability, rather than using the total number of outcomes. • Students may use the total from the whole table when they should use the sub-category total. Year 8 | Summer term | Block 2 – Tables and probability | Step 9 National Curriculum links • Record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0–1 probability scale Mathematical talk • How can you use a two-way table to calculate a probability? • To find the probability of an event from a two-way table, do you always use the whole total as the denominator? Explain your answer. • What part of the table do you need to look at to answer the question? • What is the difference between the individual values and the totals? • How do you know if you should divide by the total from a row, the total from a column or the total of the whole table? • How do you decide which row or column to look at? • When expressing the probability as a fraction, what value is used for the denominator?
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to calculate probabilities using two-way tables. Focus on extracting relevant information, identifying correct totals for division, and expressing probabilities as fractions, decimals, or percentages. Address common errors, such as selecting incorrect cells or using wrong denominators. Emphasize careful reading of questions and accurate probability notation.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Tables and probability_10_Frequency trees
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students are introduced to frequency trees as a tool for organising and interpreting data. Model how to work out the values in a partially completed frequency tree, before students independently construct one from given information. Ensure that they understand how each part of the tree branches from the previous total. Use familiar contexts that involve two-stage groupings, such as splitting by year group and then by subject. Make clear links with part-whole models to support conceptual understanding. Students should recognise that the sum of values on any pair of branches must equal the total from the previous branch. Reinforce the importance of clear and consistent labelling and encourage students to check totals at each stage to ensure accuracy. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may forget that the values on branches at any stage must add up to the total from the previous node. • Students may not label branches clearly. • Students may assume that the order of branching does not matter. Year 8 | Summer term | Block 2 – Tables and probability | Step 10 National Curriculum links • Construct and interpret appropriate tables, charts, and diagrams, including frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts, and pictograms for categorical data, and vertical line (or bar) charts for ungrouped and grouped numerical data Mathematical talk • What does each branch on the frequency tree represent? • What are the two categories at each stage? • How can you label each branch to make your frequency tree easy to read? • Where can you find the total number of people/items in the diagram? • Explain the relationships between the numbers in a frequency tree. • How does the frequency tree show a part-whole relationship? • When might you have a frequency tree with more than two branches? • Can two different frequency trees represent the same scenario? Explain your answer. • How can you check that your frequency tree is correct?
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to use frequency trees for data organization and interpretation. They complete and construct frequency trees, understanding how branches sum to previous totals. Use familiar contexts with two-stage groupings, linking to part-whole models. Emphasize clear labeling and accuracy checks. Address misconceptions such as incorrect branch sums and unclear labeling.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Tables and probability_11_Probabilities from frequency trees
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on the previous step of constructing and interpreting frequency trees, to identify totals and outcomes in order to calculate probabilities. Focus on supporting students in interpreting the frequency tree accurately, for example selecting the correct total for the denominator, either the whole group or a specific subset, and identifying the relevant branch or combination of branches for the numerator. Be clear about the distinction between finding the probability from the whole group versus from a given condition, such as “given that the student is in Year 8”. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may select the wrong total, for example using the whole group when the question refers to a subset. • Students may confuse which branch of the tree to use for a given event. • Students may identify the correct frequency and state this instead of giving the answer as a probability. Year 8 | Summer term | Block 2 – Tables and probability | Step 11 National Curriculum links • Record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0–1 probability scale Mathematical talk • How many people are there in total? • How is calculating probability using a frequency tree similar to using a two-way table? • How does the probability change if you only consider people in this subset? • Which two categories are combined to get this value? • Is the total always used for the denominator? Explain your answer. • How can you identify which values to use for the numerator/denominator? • How can you check that your answer is correct?
candidate_ss_desc: Students extend their skills in constructing and interpreting frequency trees to calculate probabilities. They learn to select the correct total for the denominator, whether for the whole group or a subset, and identify relevant branches for the numerator. Emphasis is on distinguishing probabilities from the whole group versus a specific condition, such as "given Year 8."

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Circles_9_Perimeter and area of compound shapes with circles
small_step_name: Perimeter and area of compound shapes with circles
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the area and perimeter of compound shapes that include circles, semicircles, quarter circles and three-quarter circles. Remind students that the area of a compound shape can be found by splitting it into its component parts, working out each area separately and then adding the areas together. Encourage students to identify which arcs and straight edges contribute to the perimeter, and which regions should be included or excluded in area calculations. Discuss efficient strategies, such as combining two semicircles into a full circle. Ensure that students practise both leaving their answers in terms of π and giving decimal approximations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the formulae for circumference and area or arc length and sector area. • Students may multiply all the lengths given on a diagram. • Students may not calculate unknown lengths that are needed to calculate the perimeter or area. • Students may misread or use the wrong side lengths when working out unknown lengths of compound shapes. Year 8 | Summer term | Block 3 – Circles | Step 9 National Curriculum links • Calculate and solve problems involving: perimeters of 2-D shapes (including circles), areas of circles and composite shapes • Derive and apply formulae to calculate and solve problems involving: perimeter and area of triangles, parallelograms, trapezia, volume of cuboids (including cubes) and other prisms (including cylinders) Mathematical talk • What shapes make up the compound shape? • Why is it helpful to split a compound shape into its component parts when calculating area? • When can two semicircles be treated as one full circle and when can they not? • How can you work out the unknown lengths needed to find the area of the compound shape? • Do you need to split the shape into component parts to work out its perimeter? Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different about a rectangle with a semicircle cut out of it and a rectangle with a semicircle added to it? • What are the units of the answer? • How can you check that your answer is correct?
candidate_ss_desc: Students calculate the area and perimeter of compound shapes involving circles, semicircles, quarter circles, and three-quarter circles. They split shapes into parts, calculate each area, and sum them. Students identify arcs and edges for perimeter calculations, practice using π, and give decimal approximations. They address common errors, such as confusing formulae and misreading lengths.

small_step_id: Year 9_12-13_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_1_Solve equations with squares and square roots
small_step_name: Solve equations with squares and square roots
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of square numbers and square roots, together with their knowledge of solving equations, to solve equations with square numbers and square roots. Recap calculating square numbers and their square roots. Students apply this knowledge to solve equations that involve squares and square roots, for example x2 = 16 or x = 5. Emphasise the use of inverse operations to solve the equations and highlight why x2 = 16 has two solutions: x = 4 and x = −4. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_9_Independent events
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore independent events. It can be helpful to introduce the idea through a sample space diagram, for example for rolling two dice, where all possible outcomes can be listed and favourable cases counted. Draw students’ attention to how this method produces the same result as multiplying the separate probabilities, for example 1 2 × 1 6 = 1 12 for rolling an even number on one dice and a 5 on the other. Using diagrams provides opportunities for students to develop accurate reasoning. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_10_Probabilities from Venn diagrams
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore probabilities using Venn diagrams. Recap the regions of a Venn diagram, clarifying how each represents a distinct group within the data. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_9_Describe a translation
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students describe a translation using a column vector. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_10_Reflection

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_11_Find the result of a series of transformations (E)

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Algebraic manipulation_5_Factorise into a single bracket

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Angles_2_Angles in triangles and quadrilaterals

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Angles_3_Exterior angles of a polygon

candidate_ss_desc: In this step, students use reasoning to prove geometric facts. They revisit angle facts and build reasoning chains, such as “alternate angles are equal” or “angles in a triangle sum to 180°.” Students must justify each step and ensure proofs apply universally. They identify errors in examples and avoid assumptions from diagrams.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_1_Pie charts
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning from Year 8 on drawing and interpreting pie charts. Remind students that a pie chart represents a whole split into parts, with each sector showing a fraction of the total and all sectors summing to 360°. Make clear links between proportions, fractions and angles to show how they describe the same information. Emphasise the accurate use of a protractor when constructing sectors and highlight the importance of clear labelling. Introduce data given as percentages, fractions or bar charts for conversion into a pie chart. Encourage students to interpret pie charts by identifying key categories and, when comparing two charts, recognising that without totals only proportions can be compared. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may use the frequency as the angle size instead of working out the angle. • Students may not label the sectors. • When comparing two pie charts, students may assume equal sectors in different pie charts always represent the same frequency. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 1 Mathematical talk • What is the total frequency of the data set? • How can we calculate the angle for one category if we know its frequency and the total? • How does using the formula sector angle = frequency total × 360° calculate the number of degrees that is proportional to the total? • How can percentages be used to calculate sector angles? • How can you tell which category represents the greatest/least proportion of the whole? • If you know the angle of a sector on a pie chart, how can you work out what fraction of the whole this represents? • How could you work out how many students the sector represents if the total is ? candidate_ss_desc: Students review drawing and interpreting pie charts, emphasizing that pie charts represent a whole divided into parts, with sectors summing to 360°. They learn to convert data from percentages, fractions, or bar charts into pie charts, using a protractor accurately and labeling clearly. Students interpret pie charts by comparing proportions, not frequencies, across different charts.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_2_Time series graphs
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 7 learning on drawing and interpreting time series graphs. Remind them that these graphs show changes over time and require clearly labelled axes for accurate interpretation. Emphasise that time is always plotted on the horizontal axis and that equal intervals are essential. Encourage students to discuss upward or downward trends, along with periods of stability. Emphasise that while time series graphs highlight overall trends, short-term fluctuations may not always reflect the longer-term trend. Discuss with students how time series graphs with points joined by solid lines imply that it is possible to estimate information between data points, while points joined by dashed lines imply that the data between these points is not reliable. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may focus on specific points on a graph rather than the overall trends. • Students may assume that trends will always be consistent. • Students may use solid lines instead of dashed lines or vice versa. Explain your answer. • Is there a point that does not fit the general pattern? Why might that be? • Can the time series graph be used to estimate between data points? Explain your answer. • What similarities and what differences do you notice when comparing these two time series graphs? H National Curriculum links • Interpret and construct tables and line graphs for time series data
candidate_ss_desc: Students revisit Year 7 concepts on time series graphs, focusing on changes over time with clearly labelled axes. Time is plotted on the horizontal axis with equal intervals. Discuss trends, stability, and short-term fluctuations. Solid lines suggest interpolation between points, while dashed lines indicate unreliable data. Address misconceptions about trends and line types.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_3_Frequency polygons
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret frequency polygons. Begin by modelling how to construct a frequency polygon by identifying the midpoint of each class interval, plotting these points and joining them with straight lines. Highlight that the horizontal axis shows data from the class intervals as a continuous scale and the vertical axis shows the frequencies. Discuss with students why midpoints of the class intervals are used to plot the data on the horizontal axis and to describe what the shape of the frequency polygon shows, such as increases or decreases in the data. Model how to compare two frequency polygons on the same axes and explain how the overall shape helps students interpret and compare different distributions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may plot the class boundaries rather than the midpoint. • Students may join the first and last points to form a polygon. • Students may draw bars instead of a polygon. • Students may incorrectly join the points using a curve instead of straight lines. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 3 Mathematical talk • What is the difference between a midpoint and an endpoint? • Given the boundaries of a class interval, how do you work out the midpoint? • Why do we plot the midpoint instead of the class boundaries? • How does the scale on a set of axes affect how a frequency polygon looks? • What does the steepest part of the polygon tell you about the data? • Does the line between two points represent actual data or an estimate? Explain how you know. H National Curriculum links • Interpret, analyse and compare the distributions of data sets from univariate empirical distributions through: appropriate graphical representation involving discrete, continuous and grouped data, {including box plots}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to draw and interpret frequency polygons by plotting midpoints of class intervals and connecting them with straight lines. The horizontal axis represents continuous data, and the vertical axis shows frequencies. Discuss the significance of midpoints and how the shape of frequency polygons reveals data trends. Address common errors like plotting boundaries or using curves.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_4_Stem-and-leaf diagrams
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams. Begin by explaining that these diagrams organise numerical data, using the stem to show place value and the leaf to show the final digit, allowing all values to remain visible. Emphasise that including a clear key is essential so the data can be correctly interpreted. Model how to organise the data, select a suitable stem, and record each leaf clearly so digits align. Revisit how to calculate averages and the range by finding the difference between the greatest and smallest values in the set. Include examples with decimal values, such as 7|3 representing 7.3 As students develop confidence, introduce back-to-back stem- and-leaf diagrams to compare two data sets. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write leaves out of order instead of listing them from smallest to largest. • Students may forget to include a key, which can make it difficult to interpret the values represented. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 4 Mathematical talk • What does the stem represent in this diagram? How do you know? • Why do we list the leaves in ascending order rather than the order they were collected? • Why is a key important when interpreting the values from a stem-and-leaf diagram? • What is the smallest value and what is the largest? How do you know? • What does the length of each row suggest about the distribution of values? • How would this diagram change if the data included decimals? • When might a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram be useful? H National Curriculum links • Interpret, analyse and compare the distributions of data sets from univariate empirical distributions through: appropriate graphical representation involving discrete, continuous and grouped data, {including box plots}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams, using the stem for place value and the leaf for the final digit. Emphasize the importance of a clear key for accurate interpretation. Teach organizing data, selecting stems, and aligning leaves. Include examples with decimals and introduce back-to-back diagrams for comparing data sets. Address common errors like unordered leaves and missing keys.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_5_Draw histograms
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to represent grouped data as a histogram. Highlight that the area of each bar of a histogram represents the frequency and provide opportunities for students to explore links between the class width and height of each bar. Explain that the height of each bar is the frequency density and explore the effect of using different scales for the frequency density axis. If appropriate, students can also explore creating their own axis or using different classes within a given data set. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may draw bars with equal widths even when class intervals differ. • Students may plot frequency instead of frequency density on the vertical axis. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 5 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different between a histogram and a bar chart? • What does the height of each bar represent? • If we know the class width and the frequency, how can we calculate the frequency density? • Why do we record frequency density rather than frequency on the vertical axis? • How does class width affect the appearance of the bars? • How can you check that the area of a bar correctly represents the frequency? • Where do the class intervals begin and end on the horizontal axis? • If the width of a class interval is doubled, what must happen to its height for the area to remain correct? H National Curriculum links • {construct and interpret diagrams for grouped discrete data and continuous data, i.e. histograms with equal and unequal class intervals and cumulative frequency graphs, and know their appropriate use}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to represent grouped data as a histogram, understanding that each bar's area represents frequency. They explore the relationship between class width and bar height, where height is frequency density. Students may create axes or use different classes. Common errors include equal bar widths for differing intervals and plotting frequency instead of frequency density.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_6_Interpret histograms
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of drawing histograms to now interpret them. Recap that histograms show continuous data and that the area of each bar represents frequency. Guide students to examine a single bar and identify what they know, such as the class boundaries and the height. Ask students how these two features could be used to calculate the frequency. Support students to derive the relationship, frequency = frequency density × class width. Provide opportunities to estimate values within an interval, including estimating a value for the median by accumulating frequencies. Encourage students to express parts of the distribution as fractions and percentages once they have calculated the total frequency. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe the frequency is represented by the height of the bar rather than the area. • Students may use class midpoints rather than class boundaries when estimating values. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 6 Mathematical talk • What does the area of each bar represent? • Why is the height alone not enough to work out the frequency? • If you know the class width and the frequency density, how can you work out the frequencies? • How can you work out the frequency of each class from the histogram? • How can you work out the total frequency represented by the diagram? • How can you identify the class that contains the median? • If we know the total frequency, how can you find the fraction or percentage of the data that lies in a certain interval? • How can you estimate the median on a histogram? H National Curriculum links • {construct and interpret diagrams for grouped discrete data and continuous data, i.e. histograms with equal and unequal class intervals and cumulative frequency graphs, and know their appropriate use}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to interpret histograms by recognizing that the area of each bar represents frequency. They calculate frequency using the formula: frequency = frequency density × class width. Students estimate values within intervals, including the median, and express data as fractions and percentages. Address misconceptions, such as confusing bar height with frequency.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_7_Draw cumulative frequency diagrams
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore how cumulative frequency diagrams are constructed from grouped data. Begin by discussing how the total builds as we add on the frequency from each class interval and guide students to recognise that cumulative frequency represents a running total. Highlight that these totals are plotted at the upper boundary of the class interval. Ask students to discuss the shape of the diagram, noticing that it can rise or stay level but never fall. Highlight that a cumulative frequency diagram can be plotted with either a smooth curve or straight line segments. It can be helpful to demonstrate the plotting process under a visualiser so students can watch each step clearly as the cumulative frequency diagram is formed. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may plot cumulative frequencies at the midpoint of class boundaries instead of the upper boundaries. • Students may plot frequencies from a given table rather than a cumulative frequency. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 7 Mathematical talk • What does the cumulative frequency tell us about the data up to a given point? • How does adding each class frequency change the cumulative total? • Are cumulative frequency diagrams always plotted at the upper boundary? Explain your answer. • Can the shape of a cumulative frequency diagram show a decrease? Why or why not? • How are the plotted points joined? • What is the same and what is different between a frequency polygon and a cumulative frequency diagram? H National Curriculum links • {construct and interpret diagrams for grouped discrete data and continuous data, i.e. histograms with equal and unequal class intervals and cumulative frequency graphs and know their appropriate use}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to construct cumulative frequency diagrams from grouped data by plotting cumulative totals at the upper boundary of class intervals. These diagrams can rise or stay level but never fall, and are plotted with smooth curves or straight lines. Emphasize plotting cumulative frequencies correctly and address common errors, such as incorrect plotting points.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_8_Interpret cumulative frequency diagrams
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of cumulative frequency diagrams by interpreting the data shown. Remind students that each plotted point represents a cumulative total. Guide students to identify an estimate for the median and lower and upper quartiles by finding 25%, 50% and 75% of the total frequency and locating these values on the curve. Students then calculate the interquartile range by subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile. They should also be able to compare two cumulative frequency diagrams by considering the median and interquartile range and deduce what these comparisons indicate. Encourage accurate reading of values by drawing horizontal and vertical lines and discuss why this method is more reliable than estimating by eye. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may attempt to find quartiles using the horizontal axis instead of the cumulative frequency axis. • Students may read values directly from the curve without drawing horizontal and vertical lines, resulting in inaccuracies. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What does each plotted point represent on a cumulative frequency diagram? • How do we know where to find 25%, 50% and 75% of the data? • Why are the values for the median, upper and lower quartiles only an estimate? • What does the interquartile range tell us about the distribution of the data? • What does the graph tell us about the value below which 10% of the data lies? • Why can’t the range be identified from a grouped frequency table or a cumulative frequency table? candidate_ss_desc: Students interpret cumulative frequency diagrams by identifying the median and quartiles at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the total frequency. They calculate the interquartile range and compare diagrams using median and interquartile range. Emphasize accurate reading using horizontal and vertical lines. Address misconceptions like using the wrong axis or estimating values without lines.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_9_Box plots
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to represent the distribution of data sets by drawing box plots. Highlight that a box plot is formed from 5 values from a given data set: the median, the upper and lower quartiles and the minimum and maximum values. Use of a visualiser is recommended when modelling how to draw a box plot. Students can also explore the relationships between data represented on a cumulative frequency diagram and a box plot and identify quartiles carefully before drawing a box plot. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misinterpret scales when drawing box plots. • Students may not recognise that they need to calculate missing values needed to draw a box plot. For example, if they are given the range and the lowest value, they need to work out the maximum value. candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to represent data distributions by drawing box plots using five key values: median, upper and lower quartiles, and minimum and maximum values. They explore relationships between cumulative frequency diagrams and box plots, identifying quartiles accurately. Emphasis is on avoiding scale misinterpretations and calculating missing values.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_10_Compare distributions using box plots (E)
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to compare distributions using box plots. Remind students that a box plot summarises a data set using the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum values, allowing two or more distributions to be compared quickly on the same scale. Emphasise that comparisons should focus on a measure of average (median) and spread (range or interquartile range). Highlight that the relative positions of the medians can be used to decide which data set has the higher typical value. Encourage students to compare lengths of the boxes to judge differences in the interquartile ranges and discuss which data set shows greater consistency. Highlight the importance of using the same continuous scale so that comparisons are valid. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may draw incorrect conclusions, for example interpreting a larger range as an average or vice versa. • Students may incorrectly interpret the interquartile range or range, for example thinking a larger interquartile range is ‘better’. candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to compare distributions using box plots, summarizing data with minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum values. Focus on comparing medians for typical values and box lengths for interquartile ranges to assess consistency. Ensure comparisons use the same scale. Address misconceptions like confusing range with average or misinterpreting interquartile range significance.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_1_Understand and represent vectors
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of vectors beyond the context of translating shapes, which they previously encountered in Year 9. This step will focus on interpreting column vectors and representing vectors as diagrams. Remind students that the top number in a column vector represents the horizontal direction, while the bottom number represents the vertical direction. It is important that students understand that a vector shows both direction and magnitude. The role of the arrow should also be emphasised, as it indicates the start point, end point, and direction of the vector. Comparing similar vectors can help to reinforce this understanding, for example by comparing 3 4 -   and -3 4   . Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect to draw arrows on vectors. • Students may draw arrows in the wrong direction on vectors. • Students may misinterpret column vectors, such as reading 2 4 -   as ‘2 up and 4 left’ rather than ‘2 right and 4 down’. Explain how you know. • How do you know which direction to draw the arrow? • What is the same and what is different about the vectors -2 5   and 2 5 -   ? • Is it possible to draw a vector without an arrow? Explain your answer. candidate_ss_desc: In this step, students deepen their understanding of vectors by interpreting column vectors and representing them as diagrams. Emphasize that the top number indicates horizontal direction, the bottom number vertical direction, and the arrow shows direction and magnitude. Address common errors, such as incorrect arrow direction or misinterpreting vector components.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_2_Vector notation
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of vector representations as column vectors and directed line segments by introducing notation for labelling vectors. Different conventions should be introduced, such as writing a vector as AB , emphasising that this represents the vector from A to B. Comparing related vectors can further deepen understanding of vectors as movements between points, for example by comparing AB with BA . Students should also be given opportunities to work with vectors labelled using bold letters, such as a or x. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misinterpret vectors, for example reading XY as YX . • Students may neglect to draw arrows on the vectors or draw arrows in the wrong direction. • Students may neglect to label vectors. For example, not labelling ‘E’ and ‘F’ on either end of a line segment to represent the vector EF . Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 2 Mathematical talk • What is the significance of the order of the letters in the vector AB ? How does this differ from the vector BA ? • Do the letters describing a vector always have to be in alphabetical order? Explain how you know. • If vector a = 3 4   what would –a represent? Explain how you know. • How can two vectors have the same magnitude but different directions? Write an example. • If CD = 2 3  , how would you represent CD on a grid? • If CD = 2 3  , how would you represent DC on a grid? candidate_ss_desc: Students learn vector notation, labeling vectors like AB to represent movement from A to B, and comparing vectors such as AB and BA. They practice using bold letters for vectors and address common errors like incorrect labeling or direction. Discussions include vector order significance, non-alphabetical labeling, and vector representation on grids.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_3_Vectors multiplied by a scalar
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore vectors that are parallel to each other. Introduce students to the concept of a scalar, emphasising that it is the value by which a vector is multiplied. Students should recognise that when one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two vectors are parallel. Begin by using diagrams to represent different vectors, for example by comparing a and 2a on a grid, highlighting that both are parallel and that 2a is twice the magnitude of a. This can then be used to build towards multiplying column vectors by a scalar. Emphasise that both the horizontal and vertical components of a column vector are multiplied by the scalar. Students should also have opportunities to explore the effect of multiplying vectors by negative scalars; for example, multiplying by –1 reverses the direction of a vector. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when calculating with negative numbers. • Students may neglect to multiply both values in a column vector by the scalar. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 3 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about parallel vectors? • Can two vectors be parallel but not equal in magnitude? Explain how you know. • How do we know if one vector is a multiple of the other? • What is a scalar? • What is the effect of multiplying a vector by a negative scalar? • How does multiplying a vector by a scalar change its magnitude? Does it ever change its direction? H National Curriculum links • Describe translations as 2D vectors • Apply addition and subtraction of vectors, multiplication of vectors by a scalar, and diagrammatic and column representations of vectors; {use vectors to construct geometric arguments and proofs}
candidate_ss_desc: Students explore parallel vectors and the concept of a scalar, which is a value multiplying a vector. Recognize that vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of another. Use diagrams to illustrate this and practice multiplying column vectors by scalars, including negative scalars, which reverse direction. Address common arithmetic errors and misconceptions.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_4_Add vectors
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to add column vectors. Remind students that a vector has a horizontal component and a vertical component and that these components can be represented as column vectors. Emphasise that when adding two vectors, the resultant vector is found by adding the horizontal components together and the vertical components together. As with previous steps, visual representations of addition of vectors can help students to build a deeper understanding. Provide opportunities to draw vector diagrams to show how one vector follows another, making the connection between the geometric path and the numerical calculation. Once learning is secure move on to more abstract calculations, such as adding two column vectors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when using negative numbers. • Students may draw vectors incorrectly, such as drawing arrows facing the wrong direction. Explain your reasoning. • Why do we add the horizontal components and add the vertical components to find the resultant vector? • What happens if we add vector a to vector –a? H National Curriculum links • Describe translations as 2D vectors • Apply addition and subtraction of vectors, multiplication of vectors by a scalar, and diagrammatic and column representations of vectors; {use vectors to construct geometric arguments and proofs}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to add column vectors by combining their horizontal and vertical components. Emphasize visual representations and vector diagrams to connect geometric paths with numerical calculations. Address common errors such as arithmetic mistakes with negatives and incorrect vector drawings. Discuss the meaning of resultant vectors and the process of vector addition.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_5_Add and subtract vectors
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students deepen their understanding of arithmetic with vectors by learning how to subtract vectors. As with previous steps, representing vector subtraction using diagrams is a helpful approach before introducing formal written methods. This can be introduced by considering equivalent calculations, such as a – b and a + (–b). Once students are confident, they can practise adding and subtracting vectors abstractly. If appropriate, challenge students to solve problems that combine operations such as multiplication with addition or subtraction, for example, 2 × 3 4   + 2 5 -  . Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when using negative numbers. • Students may struggle to represent vector subtraction problems as diagrams. • Students may neglect one of the values in a column vector when multiplying by a scalar. For example, writing –1 × 3 5 -   = - - 3 5  . Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 5 Mathematical talk • What does the arrow on a vector indicate? • What is the relationship between b and –b? • Is a – b the same as a + (–b)? Explain how you know. • How would a diagram representing a + b differ from a – b? • How can we identify vector addition on a diagram? • How can we identify vector subtraction on a diagram? • How do we subtract two column vectors? • Does the order matter when we subtract two vectors? Why or why not? • Can the subtraction of two vectors create a resulting vector longer than both original vectors? Explain how you know. H National Curriculum links • Describe translations as 2D vectors • Apply addition and subtraction of vectors, multiplication of vectors by a scalar, and diagrammatic and column representations of vectors; {use vectors to construct geometric arguments and proofs}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn vector subtraction, using diagrams before formal methods, and explore equivalent calculations like a – b and a + (–b). Practice includes abstract addition and subtraction, and combining operations such as multiplication. Address common errors with negative numbers and scalar multiplication. Discuss vector relationships, diagram representation, and the impact of order in subtraction.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_6_Vector journeys in shapes
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore different ways to express vector journeys, combining successive movements as vector calculations. This step builds the foundations needed for students to form geometric proofs later. Students learn to express a route such as AB + BC + CD = AD showing that multiple vectors can represent a single resultant vector. Students then move to simplifying expressions or comparing routes algebraically, for example, by writing a + b + 2a – b as 3a. Draw students’ attention to the fact that different routes can have the same resultant vector. Highlight the effect of reversing the direction of a vector, for example, if MN = a – 2b then NM = –a + 2b. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect the direction of arrows on a vector diagram, such as using the vector a rather than –a. • Students may struggle to find a route using known vectors. • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly with negative terms. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_7_Vectors in quadrilaterals
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their knowledge of vector journeys while considering the properties of quadrilaterals such as rectangles, parallelograms, and trapezia. Encourage students to discuss the properties of different quadrilaterals, for example, parallelograms have two pairs of parallel sides. Highlight that this means a parallelogram has two pairs of identical vectors. Draw students’ attention to the direction of arrows on diagrams and how this can affect the result of a vector journey and the accurate evaluation of vector addition or subtraction. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect the direction of arrows on a vector diagram, such as using the vector a rather than –a. • Students may not recognise properties leading to vectors which aren’t labelled on diagrams. How many pairs of parallel vectors will they have? • ‘A square has four equal vectors.’ Explain why the statement is false. • How can we describe each side of the quadrilateral using vectors? • What does it mean if two sides have equal vectors? • What does the direction of the arrow tell us about a vector? • If AB = a – 2b what is BA in terms of a and b? • How can we use vector relationships to identify the type of quadrilateral? H National Curriculum links • Describe translations as 2D vectors • Apply addition and subtraction of vectors, multiplication of vectors by a scalar, and diagrammatic and column representations of vectors; {use vectors to construct geometric arguments and proofs}
candidate_ss_desc: Students apply vector knowledge to quadrilaterals like rectangles, parallelograms, and trapezia. Emphasize that parallelograms have two pairs of identical vectors due to parallel sides. Focus on vector direction and its impact on vector journeys. Address common errors, such as neglecting vector direction or misidentifying vector properties. Discuss vector relationships to identify quadrilateral types.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_8_Parallel vectors
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore parallel vectors, recognising that vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Students may have some understanding of this concept from earlier steps in this block. Highlight that parallel vectors have the same (or opposite) direction but may differ in magnitude. Support strategies for proving that column vectors are parallel by using vectors represented on grids to emphasise the link between vectors and scalars. After this, model how to prove that algebraic vectors are parallel through factorisation. Once students are confident, move on to more complex problems where they may need to consider vector journeys to compare two vectors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think vectors are parallel if they have the same magnitude. • Students may not recognise parallel vectors involving negative scalars. For example, writing 6 2 -   as –2 × -3 1   to show 6 2 -   and -3 1   are parallel. • Students may find it difficult to write algebraic expressions for vectors that represent movement in the opposite direction. Highlight that parallel vectors share the same or opposite direction but may differ in magnitude. Use grids to demonstrate parallel vectors and factorization for algebraic proofs. Address misconceptions, such as confusing magnitude with parallelism and handling negative scalars.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_1_Prime factorisation, HCF and LCM
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap finding the highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and writing numbers as a product of prime factors from Key Stage 3. Use practical contexts to reinforce when HCF or LCM is needed, and model listing with small numbers to show why it becomes inefficient for greater values. Revisit prime factorisation using factor trees, emphasising that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation. Use Venn diagrams to organise information, highlighting that the HCF is the product of the common factors, while the LCM is the product of all factors within the diagram. Link back to listing to show both methods give the same result. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may include non-prime factors in their final product. • Students may confuse factors and multiples, particularly when using listing methods. • Students may rely on listing methods for large numbers, leading to inefficiency and increased likelihood of error. • Students may multiply all prime factors when finding the HCF, rather than only those common to all numbers. Why or why not? • Is there more than one way to express 84 as a product of prime factors? • Does the order of the factors in a prime factorisation matter? Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different between 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 23 × 3? • How do you find the HCF using a Venn diagram? • How do you find the LCM using a Venn diagram? candidate_ss_desc: Students recap finding the highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and expressing numbers as a product of prime factors. Use factor trees and Venn diagrams to organise information, highlighting that HCF is the product of common factors and LCM is the product of all factors. Address misconceptions about factors and multiples, and inefficiencies in listing methods for large numbers.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_2_Powers, roots and negative indices
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap evaluating powers and roots, both mentally and using a calculator. Reinforce that a root is the inverse of a power, and ensure students can use calculator functions for powers and roots greater than 3. Support estimation by identifying the two integers a root lies between. Emphasise that a negative index does not make the value negative but instead indicates a reciprocal. Demonstrate this using a decreasing pattern, for example 22 = 4, 21 = 2, 20 = 1 and 2–1 = 1 2. Encourage students to generalise this to show that for any non-zero value of a, a–n = 1 an . Model converting negative indices into fractions with positive indices using numerical and algebraic examples, extending to bases with coefficients as confidence develops. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that a negative index results in a negative answer, for example 3–2 = –9 • Students may multiply the base by the index instead of using a reciprocal, for example 2–3 = –6 • Students may misuse calculator functions for powers and roots, leading to incorrect evaluations. Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different about 64 and 64 6 ? • If 54 = 625, what is the 4th root of 625? How do you know? • What is the same and what is different between 3–2 and 1 32 ? • Which is greater: 2–3 or 2–5? Explain your answer • If a–2 = 1 25 , what is the value of a? Explain how you know. • How else can you write a–4? • Explain why the value of a in a–1 cannot be equal to zero.
