candidate_ss_desc: Students recap evaluating powers and roots mentally and using a calculator, understanding roots as the inverse of powers. They learn to estimate roots, handle negative indices as reciprocals, and convert them into fractions with positive indices. Address misconceptions like assuming negative indices result in negative values or misusing calculator functions. Focus on integer powers, real roots, and distinguishing exact root representations from decimal approximations.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_3_Fractional indices
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore fractional indices. Some students may have previously covered this as an extend step in Year 8. Ensure students are fluent with square roots, cube roots and higher roots before introducing fractional indices using numerical bases. Develop understanding by reasoning from index laws, for example 9 1 2 × 9 1 2 = 91, and link this to 9 = 3 since 3 × 3 = 9. Use this to generalise that the denominator of a fractional index indicates the root. Once students are confident with unit fractional indices, introduce non-unit fractional indices, emphasising that the numerator represents a power applied after the root. Extend to fractional bases and negative fractional indices by linking back to negative indices as reciprocals. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the roles of the numerator and denominator, for example interpreting 64 3 2 as a cube root squared instead of a square root cubed. • Students may attempt to calculate a fraction of the base rather than taking the root and then applying the power. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 3 Mathematical talk • Explain why a 1 2 × a 1 2 = a1 • If 4 1 2 × 4 1 2 = 41, what is the value of 4 1 2 ? • What operation is a fractional power equivalent to? • What root is a power of a half/third equivalent to? Explain how you know. • How else can x 1 4 be written? • How can you generalise a rule for fractional indices? • If you know the value of x 1 3 , how can you find the value of – x 1 3? • What is the same and what is different about calculating 2 –3 64 and 3 –2 64 ? H National Curriculum links • Calculate with roots, and with integer {and fractional} indices
candidate_ss_desc: Students explore fractional indices, starting with unit fractional indices, where the denominator indicates the root. Once confident, they move to non-unit fractional indices, understanding the numerator as a power applied after the root. Extend to fractional bases and negative indices, linking to reciprocals. Address misconceptions, such as confusing numerator and denominator roles.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_4_Four operations with surds
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students work with all four operations involving surds. The focus is on adding/subtracting like surds and multiplying/dividing surds by surds/integers. At this stage, surds do not need to be simplified beyond an integer result. For example, 3 × 5 can remain as 15, while 4 × 4 simplifies to 4. This keeps the focus on structure rather than technique, with further surd simplification developed in the next step. When adding and subtracting, emphasise that only like surds can be combined, just as only like algebraic terms can be collected, for example, 3 2 + 5 2 = 8 2 but 2 + 3 cannot be simplified further. When multiplying, model that a × b æ ab and that multiplying by an integer scales the surd, for example a × b = a b. If students are secure, you may choose to combine this step with simplifying surds further. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to add or subtract surds with different bases, for example 2 + 3 • Students may multiply integers and surds incorrectly, for example writing 2 × 5 = 10 • Students may not recognise when the product of surds simplifies to an integer, such as 4 × 4 = 4 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 4 Mathematical talk • Are surds rational or irrational? • When we multiply/divide two surds, what happens to the numbers inside the square roots? • Explain why 4 × 4 is equivalent to 4 • Is a + a equivalent to 2a ? Why or why not? • Why does 2 × 3 not give an integer answer? • What stays the same and what changes when we multiply a surd by an integer? • Why can we not add surds with different bases, for example 2 + 3? • How is adding and subtracting surds similar to working with algebraic terms? candidate_ss_desc: Students work with all four operations involving surds, focusing on adding/subtracting like surds and multiplying/dividing surds by surds/integers. Emphasize combining only like surds, similar to algebraic terms. Multiplying scales the surd, e.g., \(a \times b = ab\). Simplification to integers is not required yet. Address misconceptions like adding different bases or incorrect multiplication.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_5_Simplify surds
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of surds by exploring how the number inside a square root affects how it can be simplified. Model how to simplify surds by rewriting the number inside the root as a product including a square factor, for example 18 = 9 × 2. Emphasise the importance of identifying a square factor as the result of square rooting a square number will be an integer. Highlight that it is often efficient to identify the greatest square factor to simplify a surd. If students cannot spot a square factor encourage the use of a factor tree to show the prime factorisation, for example 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 . Emphasise that this method relies on pairing equal factors to form a square number that can be square rooted. Once students are confident, extend this to other contexts such as area calculations or simplifying algebraic expressions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not fully simplify a surd, leaving a square factor inside the square root when more than one square factor is present. For example, 72 = 4 x 18 = 2 18 • Students may try to partition a surd using addition or subtraction, for example writing 18 = 9 + 9 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 5 Mathematical talk • Why does writing the number inside the square root as a product help us simplify a surd? • What does it mean for a surd to be fully simplified? • Which factor pair includes the greatest square factor? • How does a prime factor tree help us identify square factors? • How can we check that a surd cannot be simplified any further? • Why must we identify a square factor when simplifying a surd? • What happens if we try to take out a factor that is not a square number? • What are the factor pairs of ? • What are the prime factors of ? H National Curriculum links • Calculate exactly with fractions, {surds} and multiples of π; {simplify surd expressions involving squares [for example 12 = 4 × 3 = 4 × 3 = 2 3] and rationalise denominators}
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to simplify surds by expressing the number inside the square root as a product with a square factor, e.g., 18 = 9 × 2. Emphasize identifying the greatest square factor for efficiency. Use factor trees for prime factorization, e.g., 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Extend to area calculations and algebraic expressions.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_6_Expand single brackets with surds
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of surds by expanding and simplifying single brackets, such as a(b + c) and a( b + c). Remind students that surds behave like algebraic terms and that the distributive law applies. Model expansion by multiplying each term inside the bracket by the term outside, using bar models or area models to support understanding where appropriate. Emphasise that only like surds can be combined and that surds may need further simplification by taking out square factors, including simplifying to integers or to simpler surd forms. Once students are confident, they could be introduced to expanding and simplifying expressions involving two single brackets. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to combine surds and integers, for example 2 + 3 = 5 • Students may assume a × a æ a rather than a. • Students may not simplify surds fully after expansion, for example writing 2 + 12 rather than 2 + 2 3. Give an example. • Explain how you know when an expression with surds is fully simplified. H National Curriculum links • Simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions (including those involving surds) {and algebraic fractions} by: factorising quadratic expressions of the form x2 + bx + c, including the difference of two squares; {factorising quadratic expressions of the form ax2 + bx + c}; simplifying expressions involving sums, products and powers, including the laws of indices
candidate_ss_desc: Students learn to expand and simplify expressions with surds, such as a(b + c), using the distributive law. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_7_Rationalise the denominator
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students rationalise denominators that contain a single surd, building on their understanding of surds and rational numbers. Model the process by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same surd so that the denominator becomes a rational number. For example, when the denominator is 2, multiply both the numerator and denominator by 2 so the denominator becomes 2. Emphasise that the value of the fraction does not change, only its form. Remind students to simplify the resulting fraction fully, including simplifying surds by considering square factors where possible. Keep the focus on single-term denominators such as 3 or 3 5. Rationalising denominators containing binomials will be covered later in the block. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may multiply only the denominator by the surd instead of multiplying both the numerator and denominator. • Students may think the value of the fraction changes when rationalising the denominator, rather than staying equivalent. • Students may not simplify fully after rationalising, including simplifying any surds or cancelling common factors. Explain how you know. • How is rationalising the denominator similar to forming an equivalent fraction? • What is the product of a × a? • If the denominator is 2, what could we multiply by to make it rational? Why does this work? • Why must we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same value? • How do we know if a fraction is fully simplified? H National Curriculum links • Calculate exactly with fractions, {surds} and multiples of π; {simplify surd expressions involving squares [for example 12 = 4 × 3 = 4 × 3 = 2 3] and rationalise denominators}
candidate_ss_desc: Students rationalise denominators containing a single surd by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the same surd to make the denominator rational. Emphasise that this process changes the fraction's form, not its value. Ensure full simplification, including simplifying surds. Focus on single-term denominators; binomial denominators are covered later.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_8_Expand double brackets with surds
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students extend their understanding of expanding single brackets with surds to expanding and simplifying double brackets. Model expansion by multiplying each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket, making all four products explicit. Area or grid models can help students see the structure and avoid missing terms. When simplifying after expansion, remind students that only like surds can be combined, and that surds may need further simplification by taking out square factors. This may lead to integer results or simpler surd forms. Once students are confident, they can be challenged with more complex expressions in the form (a + b c)(d + e c). Explain your answer. • Explain why 3 × 3 = 9 can be simplified, but 2 × 5 = 10 cannot be simplified further. • What do you notice when (a + b)(a – b) is expanded and simplified? Why do the surd terms cancel when simplifying? • What is the difference between simplifying a × a and simplifying a + a? • Can any of the surds in the resulting expansion be simplified further? Why or why not? small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_9_Expand brackets with surds (E)

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_9_Rationalise the denominator with more complex denominators (E)
small_step_name: Rationalise the denominator with more complex denominators (E)
source_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students will rationalise denominators with binomial expressions e.g. 1 + 5 2 Draw attention to the structure (a + b)(a – b), and highlight that this is a difference of two squares, simplifying to a2 – b, where the result will be an integer. Students will use this understanding to rationalise the denominator of a fraction, by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. Emphasise that this is equivalent to multiplying by 1, so the value of the fraction does not change. Begin with examples such as 1 5 2 – where the denominator can be simplified to a positive integer, before moving on to more complex fractions such as 3 1 5 – where the denominator simplifies to a negative integer or 1 3 7 3 + + where the numerator has two terms. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_10_Solve problems with surds
source_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their knowledge of surds in a range of contexts, including area and perimeter, calculations with exact values, and solving equations. Encourage them to annotate the problem and write down any relevant formulas.
